newsitem.title: HAITI: Preval nominates new Haitian Prime Minister.
newsitem.headline: Preval nominates new Haitian Prime Minister.

text.p: President Rene Preval has nominated Eric Pierre, Haiti's representative at the Inter-American Development Bank, to become the country's next Prime Minister, a top parliamentary official said in remarks broadcast on Monday.
Senate President Edgar Leblanc told Radio Haiti-Inter that Pierre was Preval's choice because of his understanding of government plans to privatise nine state enterprises.
"Pierre has a strong understanding of these plans," Leblanc said.
Pierre's appointment must be confirmed by Haiti's parliament.
Preval hopes to bring private investment and technology to Haiti through joint ventures, management contracts and concessions.
Hundreds of millions of dollars in loans and grants from international organisations such as the IADB and World Bank are tied to the privatisation plan.
Preval met with parliamentarians late last week to begin the process of choosing a new prime minister, seven weeks after his predecessor Rosny Smarth resigned.
Smarth told Preval in a July 17 letter that he would not continue to run the government on a caretaker basis after August 9 if Preval had not nominated his replacement by then.

Smarth resigned following demonstrations against him and the controversial economic plan. His tenure was also marked by an electoral crisis. The second round of senatorial elections was postponed after accusations of fraud in the first round.
Some parliamentarians said Pierre, an IADB official who has worked for the U.S. embassy, will be unacceptable to the anti-privatisation sector that protested against Smarth.
"Eric, a representative of the foreign-sponsored plan, will only fall into the same mess as Smarth," said one parliamentarian.

The popular organisations that called for Smarth to resign have shifted their focus onto the 1,300 U.N. troops patrolling Haiti's streets. They have called a general strike for Monday to protest a possible four-month extension of the U.N. presence beyond the end of July, when it is due to end.
There was no immediate indication early Monday of how many people would obey the strike call.
